chunks: LiPo aging and end of life. The question: Can LiPos be used forever? What happens as they age?
A LiPo battery does not last forever. Over time it holds less charge and gets worse at delivering current.
People usually call it worn out when it holds about 80% of its original capacity. Both using it and simply leaving it on a shelf cause this wear.
Think of a pair of running shoes. Every run wears the soles a little. Shoes sitting in a hot garage also stiffen with age, even if you never wear them.
Run hard, run hot, and they die sooner. A battery ages the same way: cycling wears it, time wears it, and heat speeds up both.
Unlike shoes, a worn battery can also swell, which is a safety signal.
Straight lines for simplicity: real fade is faster at the start, flatter in the middle, and has a knee near the end.
The point is the scaling: shallower cycling, lower temperature and lower charge voltage all extend the number of cycles to the 80% line.
The 100% DoD slope uses the example figure of 500 cycles; the scaling for the other curves is an illustrative rule, not a measured law.
Capacity: how much charge the battery can hold, in Ah or mAh. Cycle: one full charge and discharge worth of use. Calendar aging: wear that happens with time, even when unused.
State of health: today's capacity as a fraction of the new capacity. Internal resistance: the battery's own opposition to current.
It rises as the cell ages ("Battery internal resistance").
A phone battery is rated for 500 full cycles to 80% capacity. If you charge it from empty to full once a day, that is 500 / 365, or about 1. 4 years.
A new 4000 milliamp hours cell then holds about 0. 8 times 4000 = 3200 milliamp hours. Keeping it cooler or avoiding sitting at 100% can stretch the time. That is the whole idea.
"No. LiPos wear out from both cycling and calendar time, losing capacity and gaining internal resistance.
End of life is usually 80 percent capacity, a few hundred to a thousand cycles for LCO/NMC.

Causes: the SEI layer growing on the anode, lithium plating from cold or fast charging, cathode degradation at high voltage, and electrolyte decomposition producing gas, which makes pouch cells swell.
Heat, high state of charge, high currents and deep cycles speed it up, so keep them cool, avoid sitting full, and track health."
